purpose: Mirtazapine is mainly used to treat depression. It can also help with anxiety, poor sleep, and low appetite that often come along with depression. Your doctor may sometimes prescribe it for other conditions as well, such as nausea or appetite problems.
how_it_works: Mirtazapine works by boosting two natural chemicals in your brain called serotonin and norepinephrine, which help regulate your mood, sleep, and appetite. It does this in a slightly different way than most other antidepressants by blocking certain receptors that normally slow these chemicals down. Think of it like removing a dam so the mood-lifting chemicals can flow more freely.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are feeling sleepy or drowsy, increased appetite, and weight gain. You may also notice dry mouth, dizziness, or constipation. The drowsiness is actually helpful for people who have trouble sleeping, which is why doctors sometimes give it at bedtime.
warnings: Mirtazapine carries a warning that antidepressants can sometimes increase thoughts of suicide, especially in children, teens, and young adults when first starting the medication — so it is important to check in with your doctor regularly, especially in the first few weeks. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms. Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney problems, seizures, or low white blood cell counts. Avoid alcohol while taking this medication as it can make drowsiness much worse.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 15 mg taken once a day, most often at bedtime because it can make you sleepy. Your doctor may gradually increase your dose up to 45 mg per day depending on how you respond. It may take 2 to 4 weeks before you start to notice improvements in your mood, so try to be patient and keep taking it as directed.
